title: COMPOSE: Composing Future Theorems from Citations and Formal Structure
claim: Combining a citation-derived scientific graph with an aligned formal dependency graph lets a graph-conditioned LLM generate grounded future claims.
layout: 2 stacked panels, left-to-right flow, dashed alignment arrows linking informal and formal graphs
description: Two rounded panels stacked vertically. The top panel shows data construction. On the left is a citation graph of gray 'Cited' paper cards with abstract tags and theorem labels, arranged around a blue-bordered 'Anchor Paper' card. A gray arrow leads to a lavender 'Scientific Graph' of blue abstract nodes and orange theorem nodes. Dashed orange 'alignment' arrows curve from those theorem nodes to a pink 'Formal Graph' of Mathlib dependencies, drawn as a dense DAG of pink and orange nodes. The bottom panel shows the model. The scientific graph and formal graph sit stacked on the left. Each feeds a labeled encoder inside a large teal trapezoid, 'Dual Graph Encoder'. Both encoders merge at a circled-plus fusion node. The fused output goes to a dark gray 'LLM Decoder' box, which produces a yellow-bordered 'Future Research Claim' with a math quote. The eye goes first to the colored graphs and the teal encoder.
caption: Top: Data construction. Given an anchor paper and its citation graph (left), we build its scientific graph (center) where blue nodes represent paper abstracts and orange nodes represent extracted theorems. Each informal theorem is matched to its corresponding Mathlib theorem (dashed arrows), and the matched theorems are then used in order the construct the paper’s formal graph of Lean dependencies (right). Bottom: Model architecture. The scientific graph and formal graph are encoded by dedicated GNNs, fused via cross-attention (⊕), and used to condition a math-specialized LLM decoder that generates a future research claim.
abstract: A plausible future mathematical claim must satisfy two constraints: it should follow the direction of prior work and respect the formal dependencies that constrain what can validly follow. Existing approaches typically model only one of these sources, producing claims that are either weakly grounded or insufficiently motivated. We introduce grounded future mathematical generation, where the goal is to generate a plausible future theorem-like claim for an anchor paper using two complementary sources of context: its scientific citation graph and aligned formal theorem dependency graph. To address this setting, we propose COMPOSE, a dual-graph framework that conditions a language model on both scientific citation context and formal theorem structure. To support this setting, we construct a dataset of 108K paired scientific-formal graph examples from arXiv and Mathlib, together with a benchmark of 47K future papers from 2024--2025. Experiments show that COMPOSE outperforms strong baselines on retrieval to real future papers and achieves the best overall performance under LLM-judge evaluation, producing more grounded and mathematically richer outputs. These results show that future mathematical generation benefits from combining scientific context with formal structure. Project page is available at https://david-busbib.github.io/COMPOSE-page/.
